def.complaint: Vomiting since yesterday, drowsy, breathing fast
def.history: {first} has had type 1 diabetes since age 19. She ran out of insulin 4 days ago and could not buy more. Vomiting since yesterday evening with central abdominal pain; drowsy since this afternoon. No fever, cough or urinary symptoms. Brought in by her husband at 02:10.
def.exam: Drowsy, GCS 13. Dry tongue, sunken eyes. Deep sighing respiration, ketotic breath. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding. Chest clear.

source.label: Composite teaching case based on open-access DKA case reports

routes.label: added to each litre of IV fluid

caseHarmList.reason: She is severely volume depleted. A diuretic worsens shock and kidney injury.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th ed.

lytes.value: Na 131 · K 4.7 · Urea 58 mg/dL · Creat 1.6 mg/dL

nurseNote.text: Drowsy but answers to name. Vomited twice in ER. Husband says she ran out of insulin.
Feeling better, talking. Urine 450 mL since admission. Asked for water.
Feeling better, talking. Urine 400 mL since admission. Says her legs feel heavy.
Still drowsy. Only 60 mL urine since admission. Lips dry.
No better. Vomited twice more. Breathing still deep and fast.
Sweaty and shaky at 07:30. Sugar dropping fast on the chart.
A little more alert. Urine 200 mL since admission.
Eating breakfast. No complaints. Asking when she can go home.
nurseNote.highlight: Asking when she can go home.

ecg.value: Sinus tachycardia. Flat T waves, U waves.

nurseNote.text: Complaining of palpitations and leg weakness. ECG done: flat T waves, U waves.
Found sweaty and confused at 05:00, GRBS 2.9. Gave 10% glucose as per hypo protocol.
Vomiting again since midnight. Breathing fast. Drip was taken down yesterday.
Sitting up. Took some tea. Still a bit nauseated.
GCS dropped to 10, BP 84/50. ICU team called and accepted transfer.

D2_icu.outcomeNote: Severe DKA progressed without adequate insulin and fluids.

nurseNote.text: Doing her own insulin with the diabetes educator. Ready for discharge.
Well now. Stayed an extra day for monitoring after the problem on day 2.
Restarted on the drip on day 3 after ketones came back. Settled now.

ecg.value: Sinus tachycardia. Flat T waves, U waves.

nurseNote.text: Runs of ventricular tachycardia on the monitor. K+ 2.7. Moved to CCU.
Arrested within minutes of the potassium injection. CPR for 40 minutes. Not revived.

H_arrest.outcomeNote: Undiluted potassium given as an IV push.

ecg.value: Sinus tachycardia. Flat T waves, U waves.

nurseNote.text: Seizure. GRBS 1.4, K+ 2.6. ICU called.

H_hypo.outcomeNote: A dose in the dangerous range was given after the nurse questioned it.

nurseNote.text: Short of breath, frothy sputum, crackles to mid-zones. SpO2 86% on air. ICU called.

H_overload.outcomeNote: IV fluid was run at a dangerous rate after the nurse questioned it.

nurseNote.text: Serious reaction after the high dose. BP falling. ICU review.

H_adverse.outcomeNote: A drug was given in the dangerous range after the nurse questioned it.

nurseNote.text: BP 78/44 after the diuretic, no urine for 3 hours. ICU transfer.

H_shock.outcomeNote: A loop diuretic was given to a volume-depleted patient.

transitions.headline: 6 hours later
transitions.scene: Ward round. Night nurse handing over.

debrief.text: Fluid first. A litre of 0.9% saline in the first hour restores circulating volume, then slower bags.

Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th ed.

debrief.text: Not enough fluid. She is around 6 L down; insulin without volume replacement keeps her shocked and the kidneys dry.

Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care

debrief.text: Fixed-rate IV insulin at about 0.1 U/kg/h, no bolus needed.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care

debrief.text: Rate too high. Glucose and potassium fall too fast; 0.1 U/kg/h is enough.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

debrief.text: An IV insulin bolus is not needed when a fixed-rate infusion is started promptly.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care

debrief.text: Subcutaneous insulin alone is not reliable in severe DKA with poor perfusion. Use an IV infusion.

cite.source: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care
Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th ed.

debrief.text: Potassium added. K+ 4.6 is in the 3.5 to 5.5 range, so add 40 mmol/L to each litre once urine is flowing.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care

debrief.text: No potassium. K+ 4.6 looks normal but total body potassium is low; insulin drives it into cells and it falls within hours.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care
Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th ed.

debrief.text: Continuing long-acting insulin alongside the infusion prevents rebound when the drip stops.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

debrief.text: Bicarbonate is not recommended at pH 7.08. It worsens hypokalaemia and gives no proven benefit above pH 7.0.

cite.source: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS), Diabetes Care
JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

debrief.text: No evidence of infection here (CRP 6, clear chest, clean urine). The trigger was missed insulin.

debrief.text: Hourly glucose and regular VBG with K+ are the minimum for safe titration.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

debrief.text: Without hourly glucose and regular K+ checks, a falling potassium or glucose is found late.

vivaQuestion.q: Why must potassium be replaced in DKA even when serum K+ is normal on arrival?
vivaQuestion.a: Osmotic diuresis and vomiting deplete total body potassium. Acidosis and lack of insulin shift potassium out of cells, so the serum level looks normal or high. Insulin and correction of acidosis move potassium back into cells, and serum K+ falls quickly unless it is replaced.

cite.source: JBDS-IP: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th ed.
